newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: East Timor Nobel winner dismisses Suharto trip.
newsitem.headline: East Timor Nobel winner dismisses Suharto trip.

text.p: East Timorese resistance campaigner Jose Ramos-Horta, joint winner of this year's Nobel peace prize, on Tuesday dismissed a visit to his homeland by Indonesian President Suharto as a publicity stunt.
The veteran Indonesian leader flew to the former Portuguese colony on Tuesday and was to visit a 27-metre statue of Jesus Christ that has been built outside the capital, Dili.

But Ramos-Horta said the people of East Timor needed no help from Indonesia to build statues of Christ and added that the statue's height was a reference to the 27 provinces claimed by Indonesia -- including East Timor.

"The Timorese have been Catholics for centuries and do not require the support of the Indonesian government to build a statue 27 metres high, with 27 steps leading up to it, to show we are good Catholics," Ramos-Horta told a news conference.
"We know that Jesus Christ was not 27 metres tall and it is simply a joke in poor taste for Indonesia to do this," he added.
"We believe it is a publicity stunt to signal Indonesia's sovereignty over East Timor, to prevent or counter international support for East Timor. But we believe it is backfiring."
Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 after the abrupt departure of its Portuguese colonisers and annexed it the following year, in a move never recognised by the United Nations.

Ramos-Horta, who fled East Timor three days before the invasion and has since served as the resistance movement's international spokesman, shared the Nobel prize with East Timor's outspoken Catholic bishop, Carlos Belo.
According to reports from Dili said Suharto met and shook hands with Belo during his whirlwind visit, although the two did not appear to exchange any words.
Ramos-Horta, a 46-year-old who lectures in diplomacy at a Sydney university, has been dismissed by Indonesia as a "political adventurist" with little or no support back home.
Ramos-Horta said Indonesian officials had waged a long campaign to discredit him.
A right-wing group, the Sparrow Unit, had sent several death threats via electronic mail claiming to have 200 commandoes ready to liquidate him by the end of this year, he added.
"We took it as psychological pressure, we did not take it too seriously, but none of us is risk free," he said.
Ramos-Horta, who has Australian residency rights, is due to meet Foreign Minister Alexander Downer at the end of this month after a visit by the Australian minister to Indonesia.

Since learning of his Nobel honour, he has spent a lot of time trying to pressure the Australians into pushing for some kind of political pressure on the East Timor issue. Long-running and irregular talks between Portugal and Indonesia under the auspices of the United Nations have produced no results yet.
Ramos-Horta said he did not expect Australia to take on Indonesia by itself, but it could work with the United States, Canada and European Union to put pressure on Jakarta.
